ViewCastLK is a pre-publication forecasting tool for Sri Lankan YouTube content. A creator describes a video they intend to publish — its category, title, planned duration, audio language and the channel it will appear on — and receives projected cumulative view counts at day 7, day 14, day 21 and day 30 after publication, each accompanied by a range, together with publishing recommendations grounded in observed Sri Lankan publishing patterns. Behind that single interaction the system runs a continuous collection pipeline that tracks a roster of country-verified Sri Lankan channels, discovers their new uploads and re-records engagement statistics on a repeating schedule, building the day-by-day history from which the forecasting model is trained. The architectural problem this document addresses is not the forecast itself but the fact that the video does not exist at the moment the forecast is requested. Every architectural decision recorded here follows from that single constraint.

2.1 What is architectural in this system

Not every design decision belongs in this document. For ViewCastLK an element, decision or requirement is treated as architecturally significant when at least one of the following holds: it constrains the decomposition of the system into parts; it determines how those parts communicate at run time; it fixes where software executes; it shapes the persistent data model; or it would be expensive to reverse once implemented. Applying that test, four properties of this system dominate the architecture, and the reader should carry them through every subsequent view:
​ The forecast target does not exist. At the moment a creator asks for a forecast there is no video, no

early view curve and no peer cohort. This rules out the entire family of time-series architectures that forecast a series from its own past values, and it imposes a structural obligation — enforced in the feature layer and in the data view — that no value derived at or after a publication timestamp may ever reach the model.
​ Training and serving must produce identical features. A model that performs well in development

and poorly in service usually fails because feature preparation quietly diverged between the two paths. The architecture removes the possibility structurally rather than by discipline: one shared implementation, one frozen encoding map, one published feature order.
​ The engagement history cannot be reconstructed. The data source reports only current values, so a

collection run that does not happen leaves a permanent gap. Continuity of unattended collection therefore outranks availability of the dashboard as a reliability concern, and every write into the history must be safe to repeat.
​ Everything runs on free tiers. A fixed daily API quota, a bounded database allocation and a
constrained serverless runtime are hard limits, not budget preferences. Quota is treated as a first-class architectural resource with its own guarding component.

The architecture is documented using the 4+1 view model. Four views each address one related set of concerns — logical, process, implementation and deployment — and a fifth, the use-case view, unifies them: every element in the other four views exists because some scenario in the use-case view requires it, and each of the four is validated by walking the significant scenarios through it. The 4+1 model is used in full rather than in an abbreviated form. All five views are necessary for this system, for the following reasons.
​ The logical view is necessary because the system is not a single program: the same feature-assembly
logic is exercised by an interactive service and by an offline training pipeline, and the decomposition has to make that sharing explicit.
​ The process view is necessary because the system contains both a synchronous request-response
path and an unattended batch path on a fixed schedule, with different failure and consistency behaviour. Neither is comprehensible from the logical view alone.
​ The implementation view is necessary because the dependency rules between layers are
themselves an architectural commitment, and because the repository has several independent entry points rather than one.
​ The deployment view is necessary because the software is distributed across five independently

managed platforms with different execution models, and because the free-tier constraint is enforced at the level of nodes. One addition is made to the standard model. A data view is included as Section 9 and treated as architecturally significant rather than optional. The RUP template marks this section optional where persistent data is trivial or maps directly onto the design model. That is not the case here: the identity-versus-snapshot split, the composition of the snapshot key, and the derived feature view are the mechanisms that make a training label meaningful, and they cannot be derived from the logical view.

ViewCastLK is not built in a single architectural style. It is composed of three tiers, each in the style appropriate to its own workload, deliberately coupled only through the warehouse and the published model artefact.
​ The serving tier is a conventional layered request-response architecture. A static single-page

dashboard calls a stateless prediction service, which coordinates feature assembly, inference, interval estimation and recommendation generation before returning one response. It is layered because the dependency direction must be enforceable and because the model technology has to be replaceable without touching the dashboard contract.
​ The collection tier is a scheduled pipes-and-filters batch pipeline. Discovery, statistics retrieval and

snapshot writing are separate filters operating over a stream of channels and videos, each guarded by a shared quota component. It is a batch pipeline rather than a service because it has no interactive client, because it must be safely restartable at any point, and because its cost is metered per call.
​ The model tier is an offline batch train-and-publish pipeline. It reads a derived view, fits and
evaluates, and publishes an immutable versioned artefact. It is offline because training must be reproducible and must never be triggered by user traffic.
Architectural style. Three tiers, each in the style suited to its workload, coupled only through the warehouse

and the published model artefact. Figure 2 shows the consequence that matters most: no tier calls another synchronously. The collection tier writes to the warehouse and knows nothing of the dashboard. The model tier reads the warehouse and publishes an artefact. The serving tier reads the artefact and lagged aggregates. This is what allows collection to continue while the dashboard is down, the dashboard to keep serving forecasts while the warehouse is unreachable, and the model to be retrained without any interruption to either. Those three degradation behaviours are required by SRS REL-09 through REL-12 and by the degradation-modes table in SRS §3.4.3; they are consequences of this style rather than features added on top of it.
System context. The boundary of ViewCastLK and the five external parties it exchanges data with.

Every node is a free tier. Exceeding a limit degrades or halts a background function; no path can incur a charge.
The following constraints are binding on the design. They are not preferences and the architecture may not be read as satisfying them optionally.

Quota is modelled as a resource with its own guarding component and a persisted daily ledger. Routine collection uses only one-unit endpoints; the hundred-unit search endpoint is reserved for occasional roster expansion and is permitted only above a configured safety margin.
Bulk historical scoring is a separate rate-aware batch process, not part of the collection run. Live scoring must tolerate failure and is retried exactly once.
Collection is scoped to country-verified channels as a documented assumption. No component may compute or expose a Sri-Lanka-share figure, because the input does not exist.

Classical time-series and sequence architectures are excluded outright. A same-period peer ranking is excluded on two independent grounds: the cohort does not exist at forecast time, and computing it would place the target on both sides of the model.
A compact tabular model is the correct family. Deep architectures are excluded by the data regime as well as by the hardware constraint.

The prediction path must execute within limited memory with no long-lived process. The artefact must be exportable to a form the runtime can evaluate, and the model is loaded once per runtime instance where the platform permits.
Snapshot growth is monitored against the allocation and made visible to maintainers. The tracking window is bounded so videos leave the polling set once their final horizon has passed.

The hosted scheduler disables scheduled workflows after prolonged repository inactivity and may delay runs under load. The architecture answers with the 26-hour look-back and an explicit project obligation to prevent dormancy.

This is a constraint on structure, not wording. No feature quantifying divisiveness, communal provocation, controversy potential or misleading-claim strength is computed, stored or exposed anywhere, so no layer is in a position to optimise for it.
Retention, display and attribution obligations are enforced in the data layer. Records for videos that become unavailable are marked rather than retained as current.
The decomposition follows the division of work recorded in the team briefing, so that the collection tier, the model tier and the serving tier can progress in parallel with minimal coupling.

The design model is decomposed into eleven packages arranged in seven layers. The decomposition is driven by two forces. The first is the need to keep the three run-time tiers independently buildable and testable, so that collection, modelling and serving can progress in parallel. The second is the need to make one module — feature preparation — genuinely shared between the serving tier and the model tier, rather than duplicated with the intention of keeping the copies in step.

The collector and backup packages sit outside the serving path entirely — they reach the repositories and the gateways but never the dashboard, the API or the domain, which is why they can be deployed, run and fail independently.

Roster iteration is the outer loop of every run and must remain quota-aware. Growth in the roster is the primary driver of quota consumption.
Video identity writes are idempotent because the same video is rediscovered on every traversal until it leaves the look-back window.
This table dominates storage and query cost. It is the reason the index set in Section 9.2 is specified rather than left to implementation.
Point-in-time channel features require a snapshot-at-or-before join, which is why channel state is not stored on the video row.

Short-horizon modelling is viable now; day-14 labels begin maturing in early August, day-21 mid-August, day-30 mid-to-late August. This is why training is a repeated operation rather than a single event (FR-82).
Approximately 50 MB of a 500 MB allocation, growing at roughly 4.7 MB per day
At the observed rate the allocation is adequate for the project timeline, but growth is monitored and the bounded tracking window is what keeps it linear rather than compounding.
A 20% margin. This is the number that justifies reserving the hundred-unit search endpoint for occasional roster expansion and running two of the four daily runs in discovery-only mode.
Four runs daily at six-hourly intervals
Determines the worst-case deviation between an observation and an exact horizon boundary, which is why that deviation is recorded per observation and gates label usability (FR-61).
Batching, rather than threading, is the concurrency mechanism in the collection tier (Section 6.1).
Target: perceptibly responsive; no fixed maximum (PERF-01, PERF-02)

Two external calls dominate the critical path and their latency is not controlled by the system. The architecture answers with immediate acknowledgement, a progress indication, and per-call timeouts that degrade rather than wait (PERF-03).
Design point: a small number, occasional and deliberate use
The system is not throughput-constrained. The genuinely constrained resources are quota and storage, and both are consumed by background collection rather than by user requests (PERF-05, PERF-06).
Confirms the compact tabular model family and excludes deep architectures on hardware grounds as well as data-regime grounds.

Rate limiting. The principal abuse risk is not to creator data — the system holds none — but to the daily allowance that the collection pipeline depends on. Forecast requests are therefore rate-limited so that automated or repeated use cannot exhaust the quota that background collection relies on (SEC-08). This is a capacity control expressed as a security requirement, and it is the reason live channel lookup is permitted at all: at the expected request volume its quota cost is negligible against the daily allowance (PERF-06).

This section describes how the software architecture contributes to the capabilities of the system other than functionality. For each attribute the table names the architectural contribution and the means by which it can be verified, because a quality claim that cannot be checked is an assertion rather than a property.

Continuity of collection is prioritised over dashboard availability, because a missed run is unrecoverable and a missed page view is not. Idempotent writes, a 26-hour look-back, defensive handling of unavailable videos, and a run-summary record written from a top-level handler.
Proportion of scheduled runs completing successfully and the resulting rate of missing observations, both recorded and reported (REL-03).
Nightly logical export of roles, schema and data to off-site storage with per-file checksums and post-upload verification; restore testing isolated to a temporary project.
A restore test against a separate project, confirming the backup is not merely present but usable (REL-07).

Deliberately asymmetric. The dashboard offers no continuous-availability guarantee; interruptions are not treated as failures. The collection pipeline is required to keep its schedule without manual intervention.
Run log completeness; absence of unexplained gaps in the engagement history (REL-01, REL-02).

Failure of a supporting service reduces the information content of the answer, never removes it. Only the absence of a loadable artefact prevents a forecast, and that case is stated plainly rather than filled with a placeholder.
Fault injection against each external dependency in turn, checking that a forecast is still returned and correctly labelled degraded (REL-09 to REL-11).
Publication-anchored age is part of the snapshot key, so the invariant is enforced by the store. Boundary deviation is recorded per observation and gates label usability.
Schema inspection plus a check that no snapshot exists whose age disagrees with its video's published at (REL-14, DC-11). _
One shared feature-preparation module; a frozen encoding map and published feature order; interval calibration measured before release and a release blocked when coverage departs from nominal.
The automated round-trip test on a known training row (SUP-05); the coverage and width figures in the metrics report (FR-82a to FR-82c).

All external calls are server-side, so no credential reaches a browser. Secrets are injected from platform secret stores and never committed, logged or returned. Error messages disclose no implementation detail.
Repository and log inspection for secret material; review of returned error payloads (SEC-01 to SEC-04, SEC-10).

The system requires no account and collects no personal data from creators. It stores only publicly available channel and video information. This is a structural property, not a policy: there is no store in which creator data could be placed.
Schema inspection: no table holds creator-identifying data (SEC-06, SEC-07, LEG-06).
No feature quantifying divisiveness, communal provocation, controversy potential or misleading-claim strength is computed, stored or exposed anywhere, so no layer is in a position to optimise for it.
Inspection of the feature list published with the artefact, and of the recommendation engine's permitted output set (DC-13, FR-19, FR-43).
Strict inward dependency rule; all SQL confined to one layer; all schema change through versioned migrations; a domain layer with no outbound dependencies.
Static dependency check against the rules in Section 8.2; migration history review (SUP-01 to SUP-03, SUP-10).

The model technology sits behind an adapter and interval estimation behind an interface with two implementations, so the open modelling decisions can be resolved without touching the dashboard contract or the feature layer.
Substituting the model library and confirming that no file outside the inference layer changes (DC-06).
A domain layer with no infrastructure dependencies; repositories behind interfaces; a reproducible training run recorded with its seed, split boundary and row-filter counts.
Domain tests running without a database or network; reproduction of a prior training run from its recorded configuration (SUP-07).
Exactly one run-summary record per run, sufficient to diagnose a failure without direct database inspection; a persisted quota ledger by call class; the model version returned with every forecast.
Diagnosing a deliberately failed run from the run log alone (SUP-09, FR-66).

Plain-language output throughout, with model terminology and statistical notation confined to internal reporting; a forecast obtainable from a single screen with no account; entered values preserved across errors and results.
An informal usability check with a small group of representative users, in which reaching an actionable forecast unaided is the pass condition (UR-01, UR-04).
